claim: A clandestine study circle in Russian-ruled Warsaw, later named by historians the "Flying University," gave young Poles, especially women barred from universities, secret lessons from the 1880s.
source_title: Flying University
limitations: Continuously-updated web encyclopedia entry; no single publication date. Corroborates but does not itself quote Curie; her own autobiography (H4-E02) describes the circle without using this name.

claim: Curie's own account describes taking part, as a young woman in Warsaw, in an unnamed covert circle of young people who gave each other evening lessons, which she calls a secret organization that made everything extremely difficult.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: English translation, Project Gutenberg eBook #69617 (public domain in the US); read in full across three WebFetch passes covering the full ~287,000-character HTML file. Paraphrased; the one verbatim quote taken from this source is reserved for H4-E12.

claim: Around age seventeen Curie took a position as governess to help support her family and save money toward studying abroad.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02; paraphrased, not quoted.

claim: Curie and her older sister agreed to mutual aid so each could study in Paris in turn; the sister went first, to train in medicine, while Curie worked and saved to follow.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02; paraphrased. The text does not name the sister; secondary sources identify her as Bronisawa (Bronya) Dluska.

claim: Curie moved to Paris in November 1891, age 24, to study science, and lived on very little money: a cold rented room and meals often reduced to bread with chocolate, eggs, or fruit.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02; paraphrased. A separate short biographical note elsewhere in the same volume gives 1892 for the move, a minor internal date conflict.

claim: After her first daughter's birth, Curie resumed laboratory work intending to prepare a doctoral thesis, chose to investigate the uranium-ray effect Becquerel had found, and worked first in a glassed-in former storeroom, then processed ore in a leaking wooden shed.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02; paraphrased.

claim: Curie and Pierre announced the existence of polonium in July 1898 and of radium in December 1898; by her own later account the two elements' proportion in the processed ore did not reach even a millionth of a percent, far below their early hope.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02; paraphrased. Cross-checked against the quantitative claims in the 1903 thesis translation (H4-E09/E10).

claim: Curie defended her doctoral thesis, "Recherches sur les substances radioactives," on 25 June 1903; she is widely, though not independently archivally verified here, credited as the first woman in France to earn a doctorate in physics.
source_title: Thesis of Marie Curie (exhibit page)
limitations: Secondary exhibit page, undated; the "first woman" framing is repeated across several secondary sources without citation to an underlying archival record, and is limited to physics specifically (an 1875 French medical doctorate predates it in that other field).

claim: Curie frames her 1903 published research as extraction of new radioactive substances and further study of their properties, and describes her measurement method: ionization current through air, read by an electrometer and a quartz-piezoelectric balance, applied to pitchblende residue processed in stages.
source_title: Radio-Active Substances (Chemical News reprint, 1903)
limitations: English translation, originally printed in Chemical News vol. 88 (1903); not the French original filed at the Sorbonne. Read via WebFetch through roughly the first 136,000 of about 236,000 characters (through Chapter IV) — partial.

claim: On whether polonium was truly a new chemical element, Curie wrote that she was not sure that this opinion is correct, explicitly flagging the question as unresolved while treating radium as settled.
source_title: Radio-Active Substances (Chemical News reprint, 1903)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E09. This is the one verbatim quote drawn from this source.

claim: Pierre Curie was killed by a horse-drawn vehicle in Paris on 19 April 1906; the Paris science faculty then asked Marie Curie to take over his professorship, which she accepted.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02; paraphrased.

claim: Curie and Pierre decided against patenting the radium-extraction process and published their method without reserve: in her own words, "We took out no patent."
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02. This is the one verbatim quote drawn from this source (reserved quote; see H4-E02 note).

claim: During the First World War, Curie organized mobile radiological cars and fixed X-ray posts near the front; she later wrote that the practice had saved the lives of many wounded men.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02; paraphrased (quote budget for this source used at H4-E12).

claim: Secondary estimates of Curie's wartime radiology program put it at roughly 20 mobile units and about 200 fixed posts, crediting her with training at least 150 women in radiography, and with up to about one million soldiers examined over the war (estimate, not an audited count).
source_title: How Marie Curie Helped Save a Million Soldiers During World War I
limitations: Secondary feature article; exact publication date not captured in research notes. The 'up to a million' figure is presented across several outlets as an estimate, not an audited count; no per-unit or per-year breakdown found.

claim: Writing after the war, Curie expressed doubt about whether she would succeed in building a properly funded Institute of Radium to continue the work and honor Pierre.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02; paraphrased (quote budget for this source used at H4-E12).

claim: A 1921 US fund-raising campaign organized by journalist Marie Mattingly Meloney among American women raised money (target near US $100,000) for a gram of radium for Curie's Institute; President Harding presented it to her at the White House on 20 May 1921.
author_or_org: American Institute of Physics, Center for History of Physics
source_title: Marie Curie and the Science of Radioactivity: The Radium Institute
limitations: Secondary archive narrative, undated page; read via WebFetch summary, not a verbatim sentence-by-sentence read. A separate account (not independently confirmed here) puts the campaign's surplus above target at about US $56,400.

claim: In November 1910 Curie stood for a vacant seat at the French Academy of Sciences and lost narrowly in January 1911 amid a press campaign falsely attacking her as not a "real" Frenchwoman; later in 1911 a second press storm over her private life (the Langevin affair) brought a hostile crowd to her home, yet she travelled to Stockholm that December, with her sister and elder daughter, to receive her second Nobel Prize and deliver her lecture.
author_or_org: American Institute of Physics, Center for History of Physics
source_title: Marie Curie and the Science of Radioactivity: Scandal and Recovery (1910-1913)
limitations: Secondary archive narrative, undated page; read via WebFetch summary. Contains no direct quotations from Curie herself on these events, only from others (Gouy, a newspaper, a friend of Langevin's).

claim: In the months after the 1911 scandal Curie suffered a breakdown in health (depression, kidney disease), had surgery in March 1912, convalesced privately under her maiden name, and did not resume writing in her laboratory notebook until 3 December 1912, about fourteen months after her last entry.
author_or_org: American Institute of Physics, Center for History of Physics
source_title: Marie Curie and the Science of Radioactivity: Scandal and Recovery, continued
limitations: Secondary archive narrative, undated page; read via WebFetch summary. The one direct Curie quotation surfaced here (to the Sorbonne's dean, May 1913) runs over the 15-word limit and was not used verbatim in the dossier or views file.

claim: The line "Nothing in life is to be feared, it is only to be understood" is widely attributed to Marie Curie on quotation websites, but no primary source in her own writing (letters, the 1923 autobiography, her 1903 or 1921 texts) was found to contain it; the earliest traceable citation found is a 1973 secondary quotation book, 39 years after her death.
source_title: Quote by Marie Curie (attribution-tracking pages)
limitations: Negative/absence finding: within this search's budget, no primary citation was found. Listed in dossier G as commonly attributed, not verified; never used as [quoted].

claim: In a letter to her younger daughter Eve, reproduced in Eve Curie's 1937 biography, Marie Curie wrote: "I am among those who think that science has great beauty," comparing the scientist in a laboratory to a child before natural phenomena.
source_title: Madame Curie: A Biography
limitations: In copyright; used here for this fact plus the one short quote permitted from this source, per source rules. Wording taken from a secondary reproduction (themarginalian.org); other sites attribute it to p.341 of the Vincent Sheean translation and to a July 1929 letter, neither independently confirmed here against the original edition.

claim: In her 14 May 1921 Vassar College address, Curie recalled working, with Pierre, "in a hangar where there were no improvements, no good chemical arrangements," and said plainly, "We had no help, no money," of the years before radium was isolated.
source_title: The Discovery of Radium (Vassar College address)
limitations: Project Gutenberg eBook #61622; read in full via WebFetch, single pass, no truncation reported. Paraphrased; one of three distinct claims drawn from this address (see H4-E22, H4-E23).

claim: In the same address Curie stated her central belief about funding research: "It must be done for itself, for the beauty of science," since no one knew in advance it would prove useful in hospitals.
source_title: The Discovery of Radium (Vassar College address)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E21. This is the one verbatim quote drawn from this source.

claim: Curie closed the address by telling the Vassar students it was her earnest desire that some of them carry on this scientific work, and urged them to keep as their ambition making a permanent contribution to science, naming cancer treatment as a use of radium she considered particularly important.
source_title: The Discovery of Radium (Vassar College address)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E21; paraphrased (quote budget for this source used at H4-E22).

claim: Reflecting on the postwar period, Curie wrote that a society in which an eager desire for riches and luxury reigns does not understand the value of science, and that a well-organized society ought to assure researchers the means for efficient labor.
source_title: Pierre Curie, with Autobiographical Notes by Marie Curie (trans. Charlotte and Vernon Kellogg)
limitations: Same edition and read as H4-E02; paraphrased (quote budget for this source used at H4-E12). Corroborated independently by a secondary reproduction of an adjacent passage on nist.gov (not itself cited as a separate row).
